nature-econ-844.q: What four rules about preferences did von Neumann and Morgenstern say lead a person to act as if maximising expected utility?

nature-econ-805.q: What is a deductible in insurance?
nature-econ-805.a: The amount the insured person must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim.

nature-econ-792.q: When valuing future cash flows, what two parts make up the discount rate?
nature-econ-792.a: The time value of money (the risk-free rate) plus a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive.

nature-econ-779.q: What does a person get from an annuity sold by a life insurer?
nature-econ-779.a: Regular income, often for retirement, in return for a lump sum or premiums.

nature-econ-752.q: How does a higher social discount rate affect a social project's chance of being funded?
nature-econ-752.a: It makes the project less likely to be funded.

nature-econ-755.q: Did the Stern Review use a zero discount rate?
nature-econ-755.a: No. That is a common misconception: its projections used many positive rates, while taking time preference near zero.

nature-econ-804.q: What did Milton Friedman's monetarism hold about inflation?
nature-econ-804.a: That inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

nature-econ-748.q: How does hyperbolic discounting differ from exponential discounting?
nature-econ-748.a: Under hyperbolic discounting, value falls quickly over short early delays and more slowly over longer ones; exponential discounting lowers value by a constant factor per unit of delay.

nature-econ-761.q: Why do longer-lasting assets usually have to offer higher yields?
nature-econ-761.a: Because of the effect that shows up as a yield gap between assets of different maturities and conversion costs.

nature-econ-788.a: Applying the normative approach in practice: building tools and software to help people decide better.

nature-econ-810.q: How does index-based crop insurance decide when to pay farmers?
nature-econ-810.a: It pays when a modelled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur.

nature-econ-822.q: Under constant relative risk aversion, how does wealth affect the share put in a risky asset?
nature-econ-822.a: It does not: the share does not depend on how rich one is.

nature-econ-798.q: In the St. Petersburg game, how does the prize grow and when does the game end?
nature-econ-798.a: The prize doubles each time the coin lands heads, and the game ends at the first tails.

nature-econ-815.q: Why did Aristotle and the Scholastics think charging interest was unjust?
nature-econ-815.a: They held that money is by nature sterile, so it was unjust to charge for being parted from it.

nature-econ-843.q: How might feeling connected to one's future self affect choices over time?
nature-econ-843.a: It may make it easier to delay gratification.

nature-econ-829.q: How does the Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model treat saving differently from the Solow–Swan model?
nature-econ-829.a: Solow–Swan fixes the saving rate; this model derives saving from a household's optimisation over time.

nature-econ-830.q: How is the elasticity of intertemporal substitution related to relative risk aversion?
nature-econ-830.a: It is formally the inverse: high relative risk aversion means a low elasticity and a stronger wish to smooth consumption.

nature-econ-750.q: In quasi-hyperbolic discounting, how are rewards taken now treated?
nature-econ-750.a: They are not discounted at all.

nature-econ-785.q: What is a firm's cost of capital?
nature-econ-785.a: The minimum return it must earn on its assets to satisfy its lenders, owners and other capital providers, or they will invest elsewhere.

nature-econ-826.q: Why did John Harsanyi use the original position to argue for utilitarianism?
nature-econ-826.a: Because rational agents weigh expected outcomes rather than worst cases.

nature-econ-828.q: What does Kimball's measure of absolute prudence capture?
nature-econ-828.a: The precautionary motive for saving, just as risk aversion measures the desire for insurance.

nature-econ-531.q: Which writer may have first used the term human capital?
nature-econ-531.a: Irving Fisher, though Adam Smith earlier counted people's acquired and useful abilities as capital.

nature-econ-604.q: Where does a firm's financial capital come from?
nature-econ-604.a: From its retained earnings or from lenders and investors; it is used to buy real capital equipment.

nature-econ-595.q: Why is climate change mitigation called a stock-and-flow problem?
nature-econ-595.a: Because it means cutting the stock of greenhouse gases in the air by reducing emissions and increasing carbon dioxide removal.

nature-econ-592.q: What can happen to bonding groups without bridging ties?
nature-econ-592.a: They can become isolated from the rest of society.

nature-econ-601.q: What did Reiner Kümmel conclude about the Solow residual?
nature-econ-601.a: That it can be explained very well by an economy's energy input.

nature-econ-576.q: Why does the Paasche index understate inflation?
nature-econ-576.a: It assumes consumers adjust their purchases instantly to new prices.

nature-econ-566.a: Output, spending and income of households, corporations and government, their links with other countries, and their net worth.

nature-econ-486.q: What is the factor used to convert GDP from current to constant values called?

nature-econ-586.q: Why can nominal GDP rise even when physical output stays the same?

nature-econ-526.q: How does the GDP deflator's basket differ from the CPI's?
nature-econ-526.a: The CPI has a fixed basket; the deflator's changes each year with spending and investment patterns.

nature-econ-554.q: When is stabilisation policy expansive and when contractive?
nature-econ-554.a: Expansive in a recession, contractive when the economy overheats.

nature-econ-564.a: Because conventional policy can fail in a liquidity trap.

nature-econ-524.q: What happens to interest-rate cuts in a liquidity trap?
nature-econ-524.a: They fail to boost demand because banks will not lend and consumers will not spend.

nature-econ-491.q: For a firm, how can gross income be defined?
nature-econ-491.a: As all revenue minus the cost of goods sold.

nature-econ-510.a: The minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing.

nature-econ-517.q: How are net measures such as net domestic product found?
nature-econ-517.a: By deducting consumption of fixed capital from GDP and GNI.

nature-econ-489.q: How can a traffic jam raise GDP while making life worse?
nature-econ-489.a: Extra fuel use adds to GDP, while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted.

nature-econ-548.q: What did economists use before rational expectations?
nature-econ-548.a: Adaptive expectations, where people look only at the recent past.

nature-econ-513.q: In Friedman's theory, into what two parts is income split?
nature-econ-513.a: Transitory and permanent parts, whose changes affect consumption differently.

nature-econ-482.q: What was the classical view, from Adam Smith, of how inequality affects growth?
nature-econ-482.a: Inequality boosts saving by the wealthy, speeding capital accumulation and growth.

nature-econ-571.q: Whose income does national income cover?

nature-econ-546.q: What did Keynes explain about a small fall in consumption or investment?
nature-econ-546.a: It could be magnified into declines across the economy.

nature-econ-498.q: Why does a parent's unpaid childcare not show up in GDP while a nanny's does?
nature-econ-498.a: GDP counts only the paid nanny's income, not unpaid work at home.

nature-econ-503.q: What does the five-sector circular flow model add?
nature-econ-503.a: Banks and other intermediaries that borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

nature-econ-536.q: Why does the definition of intermediate consumption strongly affect GDP?
nature-econ-536.a: Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP.

nature-econ-567.q: What do national balance sheets record?
nature-econ-567.a: The stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time.

nature-econ-034.q: What makes a game cooperative rather than non-cooperative?
nature-econ-034.a: Players can make binding, externally enforced commitments; in a non-cooperative game agreements must enforce themselves.

nature-econ-039.q: What is the dilemma in the prisoner's dilemma?
nature-econ-039.a: Betraying is rational for each player, yet both would get a higher payoff by cooperating.
